ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure is triangle ABC, A is above, B and C are below, P is located on line segment AB and strictly between A and B, and line segment PC connects to C. It is known that AB=AC, and AP=PC=CB. Then reason: Let ∠A=x. Because AB=AC, the base angles of triangle ABC are equal; denote ∠ABC=∠ACB=β, then β=(180°-x)/2. Because AP=PC, triangle APC is an isosceles triangle; also because AP and AB are collinear, ∠PAC=∠A=x, therefore ∠ACP=x. The angle ∠ACB=β at point C is divided by CP into ∠ACP and ∠PCB, so ∠PCB=β-x. On the other hand, because PC=CB, triangle PCB is an isosceles triangle, and its base angles ∠CPB and ∠PBC are equal. Since BP and BA are collinear, ∠PBC=∠ABC=β, therefore the vertex angle ∠PCB of triangle PCB is 180°-2β. From β=(180°-x)/2, one obtains 180°-2β=x, so ∠PCB=x. Thus β-x=x, that is β=2x. Substituting into β=(180°-x)/2 gives (180°-x)/2=2x, solving gives 180°-x=4x, 5x=180°, x=36°.

method.method_draft: Angle-chasing route. Read from the diagram that P lies on segment AB and segment PC is drawn to C, so angles at A and B involving AP or BP coincide with the corresponding angles of triangle ABC. Let angle A = x. Since AB = AC, the base angles of triangle ABC are both beta = (180° - x)/2. Since AP = PC, triangle APC is isosceles, and because AP lies along AB, angle PAC = x, so angle ACP = x. At C, the full angle ACB = beta is split into angle ACP + angle PCB, hence angle PCB = beta - x. Since PC = CB, triangle PCB is isosceles with equal sides meeting at C, so its base angles at P and B are equal; in particular angle PBC = beta, and therefore its vertex angle angle PCB = 180° - 2 beta = x. Equate the two expressions for angle PCB: beta - x = x, so beta = 2x. With beta = (180° - x)/2, solve (180° - x)/2 = 2x to get x = 36°.

method.method_draft: Length-and-law-of-cosines route. Normalize the common length AP = PC = CB to 1. Let AB = AC = s. Since P lies between A and B and AP = 1, we have PB = s - 1. In triangle ABC, with sides AB = AC = s and BC = 1, let beta = angle ABC. By the law of cosines at B, cos beta = (AB^2 + BC^2 - AC^2)/(2·AB·BC) = 1/(2s). In triangle PBC, the same angle at B is angle PBC = beta because P lies on BA; its sides are PB = s - 1, BC = 1, PC = 1. Applying the law of cosines at B gives cos beta = ((s - 1)^2 + 1^2 - 1^2)/(2(s - 1)·1) = (s - 1)/2. Equating gives 1/(2s) = (s - 1)/2, so s^2 - s - 1 = 0 and s = (1 + sqrt(5))/2. Now use the law of cosines in triangle ABC for the apex angle A: cos A = (s^2 + s^2 - 1)/(2s^2) = 1 - 1/(2s^2). Substituting s = (1 + sqrt(5))/2 yields cos A = (1 + sqrt(5))/4 = cos 36°, so angle A = 36°.
